highlights.title: Tapo’s new indoor security camera includes a touchscreen for video calls
highlights.summary: TP-Link's Tapo smart home brand announced a new indoor security camera that can help keep an eye on your house while you're away or connect you to family and friends while you're at home.
body: The C825 can keep an eye on your home or help you keep in touch with your family.

The Tapo C825 is available starting today for $149.99. That’s a little expensive for a 2K camera, but its tracking capabilities could make up for it not being 4K. Using a rotating base the C825 can pan 360 degrees while its camera module on top can tilt up and down up to 156 degrees. When paired with the camera’s 114.5-degree field of view every corner of a room should be covered, including in the middle of the night using its infrared night vision capabilities.

When used as a security camera the C825 leverages AI to differentiate between subjects including pets and different people through facial recognition. It can also recognize sounds and send alerts when a crying baby or barking dog is heard. The detection processing happens on-device, and videos of events are stored locally on a microSD card up to 512GB in size. No subscription is required, but you can upgrade to Tapo Care for a monthly fee, which adds cloud storage and features like video summaries and weekly reports.

highlights.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
highlights.summary: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer.
body: Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

highlights.title: Tangles Review
highlights.summary: Tangles Review: The Gay Nineties collide with a high-strung Jewish family in a shattering animated film about dementia.
body: Tangles is in theaters in New York and Los Angeles on Nov. 27. It will expand to a wider release in January.

The weight of memory is vital to the biographical animated feature Tangles, a black-and-white story about family, the queer ‘90s, and above all else, early-onset Alzheimer’s. Based on the sparse but powerful 2012 comic by Sarah Leavitt — who co-wrote the screenplay with Trev Renney and director Leah Nelson — the film employs abstractions in its margins and connective tissue, making room for straightforward drama that proves incredibly moving in its unearthing of lived experience.

They blame it, at first, on menopause, and then on Midge losing her job and her ensuing depression, but minor tasks prove frustrating and confusing for the usually gentle 50-something, who’s drawn with appropriately haggard squiggles. It takes a while before a real diagnosis tells them what might be wrong: an early form of dementia. This forces Sarah to fly back and forth between her family and her supportive, stud girlfriend Donimo (Samira Wiley), a schism of time, place and culture that slowly wears on her as Midge’s disease advances.

highlights.title: Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?
highlights.summary: The emergence of powerful vibe-coding agents and tools like Reverse Engineer Anything has caused chaos in the music gear world, leaving companies scrambling to figure out how to respond. While some, like Roland, have remained silent for now, others have embraced the modding community.
body: Companies like Akai have decided to embrace the modding community rather than resist vibe coders.

The biggest name to decide “if you can’t beat ’em, join ’em” is inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more. “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge. That includes a recently launched SDK and several open-source devices, including the recently teased MPC Sample Key.

Akai is trying to walk a fine line, offering modders access while keeping its products reliable for professionals. O’Donnell says the company will “try to give them a reset button” so “they can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”

Behringer has also rushed to cash in, announcing a slew of open-source devices. In just a matter of weeks, it announced a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller, all of which are open source. It’s unclear when any of these products might launch.

highlights.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
highlights.summary: Huang still faces questions from Congress and his own board about his romantic relationship with an alleged chip smuggler.
body: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company confronts. The chipmaker still faces multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of US export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up, and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. US Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities & Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.

highlights.title: Take-Two Appears to Be Trying to Scrub GTA 6 PC Ports From the Internet, as Vibecoders Race Toward Controversial World First
highlights.summary: Take-Two appears to be taking on the many GTA 6 PC ports currently in the works following Cyberleek’s alleged release of an unauthorized Xbox build of the game.
body: This week, Cyberleek allegedly released the executable file for the incomplete GTA 6 Xbox build they reportedly leaked the week prior, sparking a race within the homebrew scene to port the build to PC. There’s even a website tracking the various attempts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox Series build to PC.
But it looks like Take-Two is taking action, reportedly convincing GitHub to delete an entire network of 3,007 repositories via a DMCA takedown notice.

Additionally, there’s an interesting note in the takedown order that addresses the “bring your own files” defence we’ve seen so often from the homebrew community when it comes to unofficial ports of video games. As you’d expect, Take-Two isn’t in favor of it, insisting that in this case, the files the user must provide come from the unauthorized GTA 6 Xbox build Cyberleek leaked online.

According to now deleted social media posts, NotRexed, author of the Leonida project, shut it down entirely. There are also screenshots of its Discord showing users posting disclaimers distancing themselves from Project Leonida in case of a federal investigation.

highlights.title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
highlights.summary: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer.
body: LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

They asked other physicists for some of their private gems—minor but real findings they’d never gotten around to cleaning up for public display. They were asking for real work, problems that take humans at the top of the field about a day to solve.
“Our contributors had to either sacrifice potential publication elsewhere, or else undertake a small research project just for us,” Raju wrote.

highlights.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
highlights.summary: Nvidia’s place at the center of the US economy may have outweighed concerns about its CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, national security and foreign policy experts say.
body: Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs —one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

highlights.title: Dottin out to 'free ball' after historic WBBL decision
highlights.summary: Brisbane's Sarah Glenn bowls to an empty set of stumps to dismiss Melbourne Renegade's Deandra Dottin after she is deemed too slow to reach the crease and face her first delivery.
body: A bizarre dismissal in the Women's Big Bash saw Brisbane Heat's Sarah Glenn bowling to an empty set of stumps, external after Melbourne Renegades new batter Deandra Dottin was ruled to have taken too long to face the delivery.

Experienced West Indies all-rounder Dottin walked out to bat, following the dismissal of Georgia Wareham, with her equipment in disarray and proceeded to adjust her helmet and begin putting on her gloves after arriving in the middle.

Rules introduced before the 2021 WBBL season to speed up play state that an incoming batter must be ready to face - or the non-striker to receive - the next delivery within 75 seconds of a dismissal or retirement.
The umpires adjudged Dottin to have exceeded this time limit and instructed her to stand aside from stumps, while awarding Glenn a free ball.

body: “The script says Paris by dawn. The tax break says Eastern Europe,” reads another page likely to make more than a few producers nod knowingly. “‘I loved your film,’ says the sales agent. He has not seen it,” adds another.

“Every page comes from something true,” said Follows, who has published more than 600 data-led studies of the industry and is regularly cited in the press. “Anyone in the business will recognize it, and the people it’s about will laugh along without realizing it’s them.”

“‘We Make a Movie’ is the book of the year — it explains the film industry in a nutshell and in the most entertaining and funny way ever,” said Uwe Boll. “I loved it! A lot of truth to it.”

"This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook in this and future years."

body: The Body team searched far and wide to find their leading lady, Anya. Kristina Bogic, the 19-year-old who landed the role, knew there were plenty of others trying for the part. “A lot of my friends had auditioned for Anya,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter.

Bogic did four chemistry reads with Sara Boustany, who plays Anya’s best friend and secret romantic interest Elise in the series. The actress had “a bunch” of callbacks — she just kept getting more scripts. “I remember thinking even if I wasn’t in this show, I would just be so excited to watch it,” she says.

The raunchy psychological thriller has become an online favorite. Bogic felt protective over the character from moment one. “I can’t believe I get to play Anya,” the actress says. “I really just wanted to take care of her the whole time.”

Anya’s the captain of her Catholic high school’s dance team. In addition to mass hysteria incidents, the teen’s also dealing with complicated feelings for her best friend. Bogic wanted to keep the character tucked safely under her wing.

highlights.title: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
highlights.summary: “TangiMap” uses an AI agent to reprogram how buttons, knobs, and sliders are used, helping users do things like edit photos and perform music in a more dynamic, tactile way.
body: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).

We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.

highlights.title: 24 Years Later, Star Trek's Most Controversial Movie Is Officially Free on Streaming
highlights.summary: Saying goodbye to beloved television characters is never easy. After spending years getting to know them, audiences have expectations about how their stories should end. Some get the send offs they deserve, while others leave fans wondering what might have been.
body: The fourth and final film featuring the Next Generation cast finds Captain Jean-Luc Picard ( Patrick Stewart ) confronting Shinzon (Tom Hardy), a younger clone of Picard who has seized power in a Romulan coup and plans to destroy Earth with a devastating weapon. It's a promising premise that Nemesis squanders on a convoluted, action-heavy story that forgets what made these characters special.

Now streaming free on Pluto TV, Nemesis remains a disappointing conclusion to the Next Generation film series. Having revisited it recently, I can confirm that nearly 24 years haven't done much to improve it.

The best episodes of The Next Generation aren't necessarily the ones featuring massive space battles. "The Measure of a Man" explores Data's humanity, while "Darmok" focuses on two captains struggling to communicate. Neither requires Picard to jump behind the wheel of a dune buggy and race across an alien desert while shooting at the locals. Yet that's exactly what Nemesis gives us.

highlights.title: Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long
highlights.summary: The “hardest remaining problem in classical physics” gets a boost from terabytes of crowdsourced data and new ways of using machine learning and AI.
body: In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

body: Investors cheered Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, but renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale thinks they’re celebrating a mistake. He sees a company that is largely responsible for putting sophisticated technology in the hands of the country’s adversaries, at a moment when the risks couldn’t be higher. Far from a champion of American industry, he says, Nvidia is “a detriment to U.S. global industrial might.”

As evidence, Sonnenfeld points to research suggesting Nvidia’s most advanced chips have reached China despite U.S. export controls and to sinking shares of Anthropic, which he links to the realization that China’s seemingly miraculous open source AI models are, in a sense, copies of top U.S. labs’ work, even as Nvidia has insisted that smuggling is a “non-factor.”
Indeed, Huang’s return was greeted with just as much enthusiasm in Asia, The Washington Post reported. “The king is back!” read one headline from China’s state-affiliated Star Market Daily.

highlights.title: Ice hockey federation appeals against Russia ban ruling
highlights.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) will appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal against a Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) ruling to reinstate Russia in next year's World Championship.
body: Russia has been banned from competing in IIHF events since the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with the sport's global governing body ruling earlier this year that the exclusion would continue.

On 30 October, Cas upheld appeals from the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the ban, claiming arguments made by the IIHF "citing safety, security and other concerns" were "not supported by sufficient evidence".
The IIHF has cited alleged undisclosed links to Russia from two of the three Cas panel members in its appeal to the Swiss Federal Tribunal.
"The decision is based on concerns around the independence and impartiality of two of the three arbitrators on the CAS Panel," an IIHF statement said.

The situation prompted calls for Supercell to intervene, with the developer addressing the controversy on November 20. In a statement posted on X, Clash Royale warned that using AI or other tools to cheat was a “royal crime,” declaring that offending players would be banished from the Arena.

highlights.title: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship
highlights.summary: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary. The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being…
body: Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland.

Their relationship continued for 15 years and in 2025 Farrell agreed to run the Dublin marathon for EB, with the final two miles pushing Emma in her modified wheelchair; a serious physical challenge for any runner. The film shows Emma and Colin in their different worlds preparing in their various ways for the marathon. (They are in fact only shown physically in the same space in the film’s final section.) But the film also shows a candidly emotional Farrell talking about his father, Eamon, who was on his deathbed in Ireland at the time, and talking also about his eldest son James, who was born with Angelman syndrome, similar to cerebral palsy.

Jayson Tatum contributed a team-high 41 points to go with 8 assists 6 rebounds and 6 three pointers, with Paul George of the Celtics adding an additional 28 points (11-20 FG, 6-9 3P) in the game.
Anthony Davis finished with a team-high 33 points along with 13 rebounds for the Wizards in the losing effort.
The Celtics improve their record to 12-6 with the win, while the Wizards fall to 7-12 for the season.
